n: After Josiah’s death, the people of the land crowned his son Jehoahaz king in Jerusalem.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three and reigned only three months (609 BC).
Pharaoh Necho deposed him and imposed a tribute of 100 talents of silver and a talent of gold on Judah. Judah was now an Egyptian vassal.

f.g: Imposed a fine or tribute on the land.

n: Necho made Jehoahaz’s brother Eliakim king, renamed him Jehoiakim — a sign of Egypt’s control — and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.

f.g: Renaming showed the overlord’s authority over him.

n: Jehoiakim became king at twenty-five, reigned eleven years (609–598 BC), and did evil. He burned Jeremiah’s scroll and persecuted prophets.
Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, now the dominant power, came against him and bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon.

f.g: Ruled about 605–562 BC; defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605.

n: Nebuchadnezzar took some temple vessels and put them in his temple in Babylon. These vessels would later be returned under Cyrus.

f.w: the vessels of the house of the LORD

n: Jehoiakim’s detestable deeds are recorded in the book of the kings. His son Jehoiachin succeeded him.

f.w: that which was found in him

n: Jehoiachin reigned three months and ten days (598–597 BC) and did evil. The text says eight years old, but 2 Kings says eighteen, which fits better.

f.g: 2 Kings 24:8 and some ancient versions read eighteen.

n: At the turn of the year, Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin to Babylon with the finest temple vessels, and made Zedekiah — Jehoiachin’s uncle — king. Ezekiel and Daniel were among early exiles.

f.g: Literally his relative — Zedekiah was Josiah’s son, Jehoiachin’s uncle.

n: Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and reigned eleven years (597–586 BC). In his first year, Lehi began to prophesy in Jerusalem and soon fled with his family, beginning the Book of Mormon story.
Zedekiah did evil and refused to humble himself before Jeremiah, who spoke for the Lord. Lehi was one of the “many prophets” of this time.

f.w: humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet

n: He also broke his sworn oath of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, made in God’s name. Stubbornly he hardened his heart against returning to the Lord.

f.w: who had made him swear by God

n: The leading priests and people also became deeply unfaithful, copying the nations’ abominations and defiling the temple God had made holy. Ezekiel saw such idolatry in a vision.

f.w: polluted the house of the LORD

n: Yet God, out of compassion for His people and His house, kept sending messengers again and again — “rising up betimes” means early and persistently.

f.g: Getting up early — persistently and earnestly.

n: But they mocked God’s messengers, despised His words, and abused His prophets until His anger rose and there was no remedy. Lehi too was mocked and threatened.

f.w: they mocked the messengers of God

f.g: Until there was no healing left.

n: So God brought the Babylonian (Chaldean) king, who killed young men even in the sanctuary and showed no mercy to young or old (586 BC).

f.g: The Chaldeans were the ruling dynasty of Babylon.

n: He carried all the temple vessels and the treasures of the temple, king, and officials to Babylon.
They burned God’s house, broke down Jerusalem’s walls, burned its palaces, and destroyed everything valuable. Solomon’s temple was gone, just as God had warned.

f.w: they burnt the house of God

n: Survivors were taken to Babylon as servants of the king and his sons until Persia rose to power (539 BC).

f.w: until the reign of the kingdom of Persia

n: This fulfilled Jeremiah’s prophecy: the land would rest seventy years, making up for the Sabbath years Israel had neglected. God’s law of rest for the land was finally kept by force.

f.w: until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths

n: But the story ends in hope: in Cyrus of Persia’s first year (538 BC), to fulfill Jeremiah’s word, God moved Cyrus to issue a written decree throughout his empire. Isaiah had even named Cyrus long before.

f.g: Founder of the Persian Empire; conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

n: Cyrus declared that the God of heaven gave him all kingdoms and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem: whoever belongs to His people may go up — the Lord be with them. The Hebrew Bible ends on this word of return: “let him go up.”

f.g: In the Hebrew Bible’s order, Chronicles is the last book, so the scriptures end with this invitation to return.
